title: Active transposable-element copies carry slightly more rare human alleles than inactive copies of the same subfamily; about half of the excess is regional, little is specific to the cCRE segment
abstract: Copies of transposable elements (TEs, mobile DNA that makes up about half of the human genome) that are biochemically active carry slightly more rare variants than inactive copies of the same TE subfamily. This is the pattern expected from weak purifying selection, but about half of it is regional, so it is only weak evidence that active copies or the DNA near them have a function. We used 155 million single-nucleotide variants from the 76,215 genomes of gnomAD v4.1 and the ENCODE4 registry of candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs). We compared TE bases inside cCREs with bases of inactive copies of the same subfamily, matched for consensus position, copy age, substitution type, regional GC content and recombination rate. In active bases that mammals do not conserve, the fraction of variants with allele frequency (AF) below 0.1% was higher by 0.097 percentage points (95% CI 0.069-0.124; 27.3 million variants), 6.7% of the missense-versus-synonymous effect. The excess stayed in well-mappable copies (0.082), at 24-mer-unique bases (0.096), and when we ignored variants with AF>=1% (0.034). A placebo split gave -0.004. Against inactive copies in the same 100-kb block or the same 1-Mb block and subfamily, it fell to 0.043 (CI 0.022-0.064) and 0.051 (CI 0.018-0.085), about 3% of the missense effect. It was in enhancer-like and TF-bound cCREs, increased with DNase signal, and was not detected in DNase-only or CTCF-only cCREs. With local matching, the cCRE segment did not differ significantly from its own flank (0.031, CI -0.005 to 0.067). At this sample size the singleton statistic also responds to mutation rate through recurrent mutation; the AF<0.1% outcome responds 14 times less, and de novo mutations (353,300) and a two-outcome model indicate that mutation-rate differences explain at most a small part. A concurrent SCI study found that the variant-site deficit of active copies is regional; our density results agree. Version 2 adds the same-region tests and that comparison. Limits: averages over many copies; near-identical copies give inflated estimates; the cause of the regional part is unresolved.

display.caption: Excess of rare alleles in active vs inactive DNA (gnomAD v4.1, non-CpG SNVs; 95% CI from a chromosome jackknife with t(21)). A: singleton fraction, which also responds to mutation rate. B: fraction with allele frequency below 0.1% (primary outcome). Orange rows add matching layers; blue rows are the main, subset and robustness tests (local cCRE density, same 100-kb or 1-Mb region, 24-mer mappability, copy divergence, primate-specific copies, segment vs flank); green is non-TE DNA; the last row is a placebo split. Reference effects are in the panel titles.

Mutation-rate checks. A: change of each allele-frequency outcome for a 10% higher mutation rate (orange, from the 6 substitution types) and for missense vs synonymous variants (blue). The singleton outcome responds as much to mutation rate as to selection; AF<0.1% and AF<1% do not. B: de novo mutation rate ratio (orange, mutation only; 353,300 trio SNVs) and gnomAD variant-site density ratio (blue, mutation plus selection), group 1 over group 0.

Excess of variants with allele frequency below 0.1% by ENCODE cCRE class, for primate-specific TE copies (blue) and non-TE DNA (green), bases not conserved in mammals, 95% CI. Enhancer-like and TF-bound TE elements carry the excess; it is not detected in DNase-only (CA) and CTCF-only elements (the CIs include about half of the main effect).

citations.reason: Version 1 of this study. Version 2 adds same-region contrasts, compares with a concurrent SCI study, and narrows the interpretation.

Concurrent SCI study of active vs inactive TE copies with variant-site density. Our density results support its finding that the deficit of active copies is regional (copy/flank 0.998 vs its 1.001); our allele-frequency-spectrum test adds a small within-region excess of rare alleles that its tests did not address.

Ward & Kellis 2012 claimed lineage-specific purifying selection in non-conserved ENCODE elements; our within-subfamily TE test with gnomAD v4.1 finds a weak excess of rare alleles in the same direction.
